content: Dysmenorrhoea, characterized by painful menstrual cramps without any underlying pelvic pathology, is a common condition that significantly impacts women's quality of life. Combined oral contraceptive pills (OCPs) are frequently used to manage primary dysmenorrhoea, and this review aimed to evaluate their benefits and potential harms. The analysis included 21 randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving 3723 women. Eleven trials compared OCPs with placebo, eight compared different dosages of OCPs, one compared two OCP regimens with placebo, and one compared OCPs with non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs). Effectiveness of OCPs Compared to Placebo or No Treatment: OCPs were found to reduce pain more effectively than placebo. Six studies reported a moderate reduction in pain, with a standardized mean difference (SMD) of −0.58 (95% confidence interval [CI] −0.74 to −0.41; high-quality evidence). Pain improvement was also reported as a dichotomous outcome in six studies, showing a risk ratio (RR) of 1.65 (95% CI 1.29 to 2.10; low-quality evidence). This suggests that women using OCPs had a 37% to 60% chance of pain improvement compared to a 28% chance with placebo or no treatment. Adverse Events Associated with OCPs: OCPs likely increased the risk of any adverse events compared to placebo (RR 1.31, 95% CI 1.20 to 1.43; moderate-quality evidence). Serious adverse events were also more likely, though the evidence was of low quality (RR 1.77, 95% CI 0.49 to 6.43). Women using OCPs had a higher risk of irregular bleeding (RR 2.63, 95% CI 2.11 to 3.28; high-quality evidence). For women with an 18% risk of irregular bleeding with placebo, the risk increased to 39% to 60% with OCPs. OCPs probably increased the risk of headaches (RR 1.51, 95% CI 1.11 to 2.04; moderate-quality evidence) and nausea (RR 1.64, 95% CI 1.17 to 2.30; moderate-quality evidence). The effect of OCPs on weight gain was uncertain (RR 1.83, 95% CI 0.75 to 4.45; low-quality evidence). OCPs may slightly reduce the need for additional medication (RR 0.63, 95% CI 0.40 to 0.98; low-quality evidence) and absence from work (RR 0.63, 95% CI 0.41 to 0.97; low-quality evidence). Comparison Between Different OCP Regimens: Continuous use of OCPs (without a break or inactive pills after 21 days) may reduce pain more effectively than the standard regimen (SMD −0.73, 95% CI −1.13 to −0.34; low-quality evidence). There was insufficient evidence to determine differences in pain improvement between OCPs containing 20 μg versus 30 μg of ethinylestradiol (RR 1.06, 95% CI 0.65 to 1.74; moderate-quality evidence). There was likely little or no difference in effectiveness between thirdand fourth-generation OCPs compared to firstand second-generation OCPs (RR 0.99, 95% CI 0.93 to 1.05; moderate-quality evidence). The standard regimen of OCPs may slightly increase the risk of adverse events compared to the continuous regimen (RR 1.11, 95% CI 1.01 to 1.22; low-quality evidence) and probably increases the risk of irregular bleeding (RR 1.38, 95% CI 1.14 to 1.69; moderate-quality evidence). Due to limited data, it is uncertain whether continuous or standard regimens differ in terms of serious adverse events, headaches, or nausea (all very low-quality evidence). It is also unclear whether one type of OCP reduces absence from work more than another (RR 1.12, 95% CI 0.64 to 1.99; very low-quality evidence). Comparison Between OCPs and NSAIDs: There was insufficient data to determine whether OCPs were more effective than NSAIDs for pain relief (mean difference −0.30, 95% CI −5.43 to 4.83; low-quality evidence). Adverse events were not reported in the study comparing OCPs and NSAIDs. Conclusions: Combined oral contraceptive pills are effective in reducing pain associated with primary dysmenorrhoea. However, they are associated with an increased risk of irregular bleeding, headaches, and nausea. Continuous use of OCPs may be more effective than the standard regimen, but further research is needed to confirm their long-term safety. There is insufficient evidence to determine whether NSAIDs are more effective than OCPs for managing dysmenorrhoea.
